https://www.dw.com/en/grain-exports-stal.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JNL3 Novorossiysk has been one of Russia's most important ports since the 19th century Image: Alexander Strela/Zoonar/picture alliance Advertisement When Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke in 2014 about Russia's motives for annexing the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea , and thus violating international law, he justified it by saying: "We could not allow NATO forces to eventually come to the land of Crimea and Sevastopol, the land of Russian military glory, and cardinally change the balance of forces in the Black Sea area." What now? Intensified Ukrainian attacks on Novorossiysk, Russia's largest commercial Black Sea port, have caused significant disruptions to oil and grain shipments in recent weeks. The Russian navy no longer dominates the region. And exporting goods via the Black Sea is becoming increasingly difficult for Russia because of Ukraine's drone strikes. It is only possible to reorganize logistics partially. If the attacks continue at such intensity, the consequences for Russian exporters and the national budget could be significant, experts told DW. Container ships and other vessels have also come under attack Image: Igor Onuchin/TASS/ZUMA/picture alliance Novorossiysk major Russian hub for exports Novorossiysk has been a major hub for Russian exports since the 19th century and even today it remains Russia's largest port in terms of cargo volume, as well as one of the largest in Europe. Up to a third of Russia's grain exports are handled through the hub, which is located close to the country's major agricultural regions. Crude oil, metals and containerized goods also pass through the port. Recent Ukrainian maritime and aerial drone attacks have severely disrupted shipments, particularly of grain. Andrei Sisov, the head of SovEcon, a research and consulting firm specialized in agriculture, uses Telegram to follow the developments. On August 12, he posted that the Novorossiysk Bread Products Plant (NKHP ) — one of Russia's largest grain export terminals — and the Novorossiysk grain terminal had ceased operations. A day later, KSK, one of Russia's largest deep-water grain terminals, also halted its operations. Operations at a major grain terminal in Taman had already come to a standstill at the end of July. Prior to that, Ukraine paralyzed operations at the shallow-water ports of the Sea of Azov. At the time of publication, only Tuapse, the smallest of Russia's deep-water grain terminals, was still in operation. "This means that virtually all Russian grain exports via the Azov-Black Sea basin are blocked," Sisov said. Ukrainian drone attacks are doing consistent damage to Russian infrastructure Image: Vantor/Handout/REUTERS Oil exports also affected The situation regarding oil exports is not quite as dramatic but while they have not come to a complete standstill, they are frequently disrupted. According to the British news agency Reuters, the Sheskharis terminal — Russia's main oil export facility on the Black Sea , handling some 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day — halted loadings on August 14, which resumed only two days later. According to London-based Argus Media, a global energy and commodity price reporting agency, Russia could have 45 million metric tons of wheat — Russia's main agricultural export good — for export in 2026 to 2027. However, the situation in the Black Sea, through which about 90% of shipments are usually routed, will make it almost impossible to supply the global market. Sisov of SovEcon estimated that "many Russian producers will not survive this season, especially after several years of deteriorating financial conditions." Because exports have come to a standstill, surplus grain will have to be sold on the domestic market, which is already putting downward pressure on prices. Even if exports were to recover over time, there will still be problems. August is usually when shipments peak and it will be difficult to deliver anything no sent this month because terminals tend to operate at full capacity during the autumn anyway. Ukraine's desperate search for farm labor To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ukrainian grain exports also decrease The escalation of hostilities in the Azov and Black Sea regions will also be felt on the global market since Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter. Ukrainian grain exports have also fallen sharply since there are attacks on both sides. In the past month, Russia too has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships that are docked there. "The disruptions have blocked out good wheat harvests in Ukraine and Russia from accessing global market," Xiaoyi Deng from Argus Media told DW. "Both have struggled to work with alternative infrastructure, such as Baltic ports (via rail) or Danube River ports but the alternatives would not be up for full replacement." According to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think tank, the port of Novorossiysk "loaded 30% less oil than during the same period last year" in the first two weeks of August. The decline was preceded by a Ukrainian strike on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal on July 19. How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Isaac Levi, an energy analyst at CREA, pointed out that damage to infrastructure was not the only reason for shipments to fall. He said that "strikes on vessels have discouraged ships from calling at ports considered major targets." According to US business news channel Bloomberg, a Greek tanker believed to be carrying Russian oil came under attack on August 17. "If these constraints persist through August, Russia will find it increasingly difficult to simply defer shipments and make up the lost volumes later," Levi said. "Russia can reroute barrels, but it cannot reroute infrastructure. The most plausible alternatives include the Baltic ports of Primorsk and Ust-Luga. "But rerouting oil through the Baltic Sea ports would significantly increase transportation times and costs compared with Black Sea exports, while available capacity remains too small to replace significant volumes from Novorossiysk." Photograph: SFM Press Reporter/Alamy Spain ‘Escape wizard’ who has broken out of four prisons is arrested in Spain Albanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and Belgium Sam Jones in Madrid Wed 26 Aug 2026 12.22 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police in Spain have arrested a dangerous Albanian criminal nicknamed the “escape wizard” who has managed to break out of four jails in Italy and Belgium by sawing through bars, clambering down knotted sheets and even using a human pyramid to breach prison walls. The fugitive, who has not been officially named, was arrested after officers from the Policía Nacional force discovered he was living in the north-eastern Spanish city of Tarragona. He was the subject of a European arrest warrant issued by the Italian authorities. Spanish police identified the man by the initials TT, which correspond to those of Toma Taulant, an Albanian national known in Italian media as the “mago della fuga” , or “escape wizard”. Before escaping from a maximum-security prison in Milan eight months ago, he was serving a prison sentence due to end in 2048 for a series of offences including violent robbery, theft and drug dealing, according to Italian media reports cited by Agence France-Presse. “It sounds like something out of a film, but sometimes reality is stranger than fiction,” the Policía Nacional said in a statement that described him as “the master of escapes”. “He escaped from a jail in [the Umbrian city of] Terni in 2009, from a jail in Parma in 2013 and from a Belgian prison that same year after using a human pyramid to climb over the wall,” the police said. “His latest escape, in December 2025, came after he managed to break out of a maximum-security prison in Italy after sawing through the bars and climbing out of the window down knotted sheets.” According to the statement, the “very dangerous” fugitive was arrested in Tarragona last Friday, putting up “strong and active resistance” as officers swooped. “The man was accompanied by a number of his compatriots who tried to stop him being arrested, including one man who struck and injured two officers,” the force said. Police are still looking for the assailant but have recovered a Sig Sauer pistol that was discarded by one of the suspect’s associates. Once in custody, the man was found to be in possession of fake identity documents, which revealed that he had a criminal record in the Catalan city of Girona for possession of weapons and explosives. He was also found to be carrying two €500 banknotes that are thought to have been counterfeited, which have been sent to the Bank of Spain for investigation. The suspect was denied bail and has been remanded in custody at a jail in Tarragona while he awaits extradition to Italy. https://www.nhmagazine.com/our-town-lanc.text: New Hampshire Magazine Sections Best of NH Food/Drink Best of NH Beer, Wine and Libations Places Our Town What Do You Know Best Places New Hampshire People Q&A Photo Contest Essays Wills and Estate Planning Guide to Retirement Living Faces of NH Top Lawyers Health Run NH Excellence in Nursing New Hampshire’s Top Doctors New Hampshire Dentists Smart Health Culture Best of NH Photo Contest Fashion Home & Garden Calendar Fall Fun & Foliage Extras Contact Purchase Order A Copy Calendar Merch 603 Diversity Bride Run NH New Hampshire Magazine Subscribe Our Town: Lancaster is the Gateway to the Great North Woods Lancaster is home to 3,200 people, one 4,000-footer, a two-screen movie theater and the state’s northernmost bakery September 16, 2026 John Koziol , Peter Noonan, Illustrator , email Facebook 0 Twitter Bound to the east by the Pliny and Pilot ranges of the northern White Mountains and to the west by the Connecticut River, Lancaster is the beneficiary of a choice location — home to both the northernmost movie theater and bakery in New Hampshire. Magda Randall owns the Polish Princess Bakery. Rita Cloutier, holding her dachshund, Miss Tootsie, owns the Rialto Theater. It is also, like many communities in the Granite State, a place beloved by locals and those from away. These days, 3,200 people call it home. Native-born luminaries include John Wingate Weeks, who was born near Lancaster in 1860. He became a successful banker in Boston before launching a political career that included serving as a U.S. senator and secretary of war. Other transplants include successful painter and “Marlboro Man” Edward Widmayer, who moved to town in 1977. You can still find some of his works at an art gallery in town. Lancaster hosts what is believed to be the largest privately-owned snowmobile museum in the U.S. and Canada. Every September, since 1902, the town has held the Lancaster Fair. The seat of Coos County and a destination in itself, the town is a through point to the Great North Woods and home to Mount Cabot, one of the state’s 48 4,000-footers. In 1895, Parker Jewitt Noyes of Lancaster “patented the first machine for making and coating tablets in a single process, which produced 5,000 pills an hour coated with sugar or chocolate,” according to a Dec. 6, 2018, article by Michael Kitch in NH Business Review, a publication of Yankee Publishing. William “Bill” Rugh, of Pittsburgh, Penn., moved to Lancaster in 1971 to be with the woman he loved. That relationship didn’t work out, but Rugh, the current owner of Williams Rugh Gallery on Main Street, has resided here ever since. Rugh has no formal art training, but in college, he bought some prints that later turned out to be valuable. He also lucked out: While he was the service manager at North Country Ford in Lancaster, he met a customer who changed his life: Edward Widmayer. A graduate of the prestigious Pratt Institute in Brooklyn, New York, Widmayer was a successful Madison Avenue ad man. From 1959 through 1968, he also appeared in many ads for Marlboro cigarettes as one of the many “Marlboro men” who pitched the smokes. Art gallery owner Bill Rugh stands near brightly colored paintings by local icon Ed Widmayer, who died in 2010. Back then, Marlboro men “were as common as the Lassie dogs,” Rugh notes. More significant was that Widmayer, who died in 2010, lived and painted in Lancaster. Many of Widmayer’s paintings were for sale at Rugh’s gallery on the first floor of the former Lancaster National Bank. Of the 93 artists in all mediums on display at the gallery, Widmayer is Rugh’s favorite, he says. “I’ve told this to a thousand people, but he (Widmayer) is the best artist this gallery will ever see,” Rugh says. Lancaster needs more retail stores, says Rugh, noting the town once tried to lure an Applebee’s but didn’t have enough daily traffic. Nonetheless, the town has a lot going for it, despite the long winters, Rugh says. “It’s beautiful country here, a slice of God’s country, and we have a two-screen movie theater,” Rugh says. “How many towns have a movie theater?” Weeks, who died at 66, is one of Lancaster’s best-known native sons. He lived at a sprawling estate of more than 400 acres atop Prospect Mountain that offered views of the Presidential Range of the White Mountains, the Green Mountains of Vermont and the Connecticut River Valley. The estate was given to the state of New Hampshire in 1941 by Weeks’ children. A wolf sculpture on the town green celebrates the 150th anniversary of Lancaster’s 1763 founding. Weeks served as a U.S. representative and a senator from Massachusetts. As a congressman, he successfully introduced legislation that was signed into law in 1911 by then-President William Howard Taft that has since become known as the Weeks Act, considered by some to be “one of the most important pieces of environmental legislation in American history,” according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The Act allowed the federal government to purchase land to protect the headwaters of rivers in the eastern part of the country and later, in the west, too. The White Mountain National Forest, which is almost entirely within New Hampshire, is a direct benefit of the Weeks Act. While Rugh and Widmayer are some of Lancaster’s best-known residents from “away,” so are Magdalena “Magda” Randall and Rita Cloutier. Randall, a native of Lodz, Poland, arrived in the U.S. on April, 11, 2003, “with a one-way ticket, a suitcase and $500.” Lancaster was her third and final home in America, after Marlboro, Mass., and Lyndonville, Vt. Randall came to Lancaster to meet a man named Herb whom she’d gotten to know online and who later became her husband. “I fell in love with this town, the downtown and the setting between the mountains and valley,” Randall says. While she already had plans to open her own bakery, she says the late Greg Cloutier helped her clinch that goal. A native of Northumberland, a town immediately north of Lancaster, Greg Cloutier owned several hydroelectric dams in New Hampshire and elsewhere. After selling the dams, Cloutier bought properties in downtown Lancaster, including the Rialto Theater, which his widow, Rita, now owns. A state historical marker touts Lancaster’s status as the gateway to the Great North Woods. Unhappy by the prospect of looking at a fire-damaged building across from the Rialto, Greg Cloutier purchased it from the town and fixed it up. Randall’s business, Polish Princess Bakery, has been there since 2015; Randall also owns the building. Randall says the bakery’s name was inspired by the legend on a T-shirt her husband once gave her for Mother’s Day. She recalls Greg Cloutier telling her that “I want to have businesses that bring people downtown.” Business has been extremely good, Randall says, adding that, ironically, the COVID-19 pandemic helped her bottom line because many of Lancaster’s seasonal residents became permanent ones. “We make everything from scratch,” she says, adding that her typical day starts at 4 a.m. In a small town in northern New Hampshire, Randall says she is proud to offer her employees a paid vacation, sick leave and a retirement match. Her bakery is a popular meeting spot. One regular is Rita Cloutier, with Miss Tootsie, her longhaired dachshund in tow. Like the Polish Princess Bakery, Cloutier says the Rialto has been successful. She credited much of that success to the theater’s manager and her business partner, David Fuller, who, when COVID temporarily shuttered movie houses, sold popcorn outside the Rialto and also rented its marquee to the public to share birthday wishes and condolences. Paul Crane, who grew up in Lancaster, co-owns P&R Excavating with his son. The business is a short distance from Crane’s snowmobile museum. In 2015, in a display of the best of Yankee ingenuity, Cloutier and her husband expanded the Rialto, but just a little bit. Movie companies require that theaters show a movie for up to four weeks before a new movie can replace it, Cloutier explains. But now, she says the first movie can be shifted onto the smaller screen while a new movie is put on the big screen. Randall thinks Lancaster “is in a good spot and in a better place than when I moved here.” People “have discovered northern New Hampshire,” she says, and they realized that the region is “not just the White Mountains and North Conway,” which is a great community that serves many visitors and offers the full array of outdoor activities, shopping and dining. By contrast, in Lancaster, people “come here for peace,” Randall says. Some people also come to see Crane’s Snowmobile Museum, which is about a half-mile north of the Rialto and the bakery, and is home to the Eastern Snowmobile Racing Hall of Fame. The museum has almost 160 different snowmobiles, including a 1926 Ford Model T equipped with rear tracks and front skis. Paul Crane, 87, who grew up in Lancaster, says the town has a long heritage of snowmobile racing and plays an important role in the history of snowmobiles, specifically the Ski-Doo. Bombardier, a Canadian company that sold logging equipment in the Lancaster area for decades, introduced the Ski-Doo snowmobile in 1959; Crane says he was the first person to ride the prototype at the Bombardier factory and the first to ride it in the U.S. — in Lancaster. The two-screen Rialto Theatre is owned by Rita Cloutier, whose late husband, Greg, bought the theater and some other downtown properties. “I’ve always wanted to have a museum,” full of snowmobiles,” says Crane, who, with his son Robert, owns and operates P & R Excavating, a short distance from the museum. Lancaster has and always will be Crane’s home, he says. His late father, also named Robert Crane, had an insurance business here, he says, adding that before he got his own place, a newcomer by the name of Ed Widmayer rented a room in his parent’s home. Those connections are important. “And all of my friends are here,” Crane says. Cloutier credits her husband for helping transform Lancaster. “Greg was the one with the vision and I was just his support,” she says. The Cloutiers moved from Jefferson to Lancaster in 1999. She and Randall are neighbors. Crane, who is a graduate of the former Lancaster Academy, is ready to welcome visitors to his museum. “I’ve got a lot of sleds here that people have never seen,” he says. https://www.dw.com/en/star-trek-star-pat.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OqQJ Prefer DW on Google Stewart needed his agent's encouragement to take on the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard Image: Willy Sanjuan/picture alliance Advertisement For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts. In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner. Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!" In addition to Star Trek, Stewart also had a leading role in the X-Men franchise Image: dpa-Film Fox/dpa/picture alliance In love with Shakespeare Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end. His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life. Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic. Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York. 'Star Trek' offer from Hollywood In the same year, Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation." The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt . "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway." Engage Image: Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection/picture alliance Adventures in the universe But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center. In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness. Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children. Stewart was a vocal and engaged civil rights activist Image: epa PA West/dpa/picture alliance A short-lived retirement In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation. Stewart returned to Star Trek for the series "Star Trek: Picard" Image: Matt Kennedy/CBS/Amazon/dpa/picture alliance This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others. In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare. Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart! Translated from German by Sarah Hucal.
